title: The buzz in your throat
teaches: The filter: a bright buzz with harmonics taken away, as your mouth does to make vowels

blocks.text: **The sound.** Listen to old synth records and you keep hearing a voice that isn't there: a buzz that seems to say “ow” or “yow”, a bass that talks. Here is the raw buzz of the synth, and the same buzz made to sing. Nothing about the oscillator has changed; something after it has.

blocks.caption: A saw wave, and the same saw sounding like a voice

blocks.text: The clue is in your own throat. Sing a long “ee” on one comfortable note, then slide to “ah” without changing the note. The pitch stays put. Your throat is making the same buzz at the same rate, yet the sound changes completely. What changed, if not the buzz?

In 1779 the Imperial Academy in St Petersburg offered a prize (awarded in 1780) to anyone who could explain the vowels and build a machine to make them. Christian Kratzenstein won it with five oddly shaped tubes, one for each vowel; four were blown through a vibrating reed, and the fifth was simply blown into.[^kratzenstein] The reed was the same in all four; only the shape of the tube after it differed. Kratzenstein had found the answer without quite saying it: a vowel is made not by what buzzes, but by what the buzz passes through.

That is the **source-filter** idea. Your vocal folds are the source: they snap open and shut a hundred or two hundred times a second, making a buzz rich in harmonics, much like a saw wave. Your throat, mouth and lips are the filter. Their shape makes some pitches ring and lets others die away, and each vowel has two or three ringing peaks, called **[[formants]]**, in its own places.

blocks.caption: A buzz on 110 Hz and its harmonics, passed through two resonant peaks as a mouth would. Move the peaks and the same buzz says a different vowel.
blocks.task: Make an “ee”: the first (lower) peak low, the second high

blocks.text: The first formant moves mostly with your jaw: open it for “ah” and the peak rises. The second follows your tongue, high when the tongue is forward for “ee”, low when it is pulled back for “oo”. This is why you can still make out a whisper, which has no pitch at all (its source is the hiss of breath, not a buzz, but it passes through the same peaks), and why a parrot, with no lips and a quite different throat, can still be understood: the ear is listening for the peaks, not the buzz.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A voice is a buzz (the source) through a filter (the mouth).
Vowels are set by two or three resonant peaks, the formants.
The pitch of the buzz and the vowel are independent.

blocks.text: A classic synthesizer works like a voice. Start with a bright wave, full of harmonics, and take away what you don't want. This is **[[subtractive synthesis]]**, and the part that takes away is the **filter**. The synth's filter is a low-pass: it lets the harmonics below its **cutoff** through and removes those above, so the cutoff is the filter's edge. Set it high, and the sound is bright and open. Set it low, and the sound is dark and muffled, while the pitch of the note does not change.

blocks.caption: A saw wave through the synth's filter. Watch the right-hand side of the spectrum fall away as the cutoff comes down.
blocks.task: Close the filter to 285 Hz or lower

blocks.text: A low-pass filter on a synth is far cruder than a mouth: one edge instead of two or three peaks. But that edge can move while a note plays, as a mouth does all the time, and that movement is most of what makes a synth sound alive.

A filter can also ring. **Resonance** boosts a narrow band of pitches right at the cutoff, the way a formant boosts a band in the mouth.[^q-factor] A little adds a nasal edge, like the peaks of a vowel. A lot makes the filter ring by itself, and you hear a whistle right where the cutoff sits. The synth measures resonance as Q: at Q 0.7 there is no bump at all, and by Q 8 the filter whistles.

blocks.caption: The same saw, with the cutoff partway down. Turn up the resonance.
blocks.task: Raise Reso to the top and hear it whistle

blocks.text: [[Robert Moog]]'s 1965 filter, the **ladder**, was built from a stack of matched transistor pairs and could be pushed into resonance until it sang on its own.[^ladder] Its warm, rubbery sweep became the sound people meant when they said “Moog”, and later filters were judged against it.

blocks.caption: Robert Moog with his modular synthesizers. The ladder filter was one of their modules.

blocks.text: With the resonance high, move the cutoff. The whistling peak slides up and down through the buzz, and wherever it lands on a harmonic, that harmonic leaps out. You can play a tune on one held note this way, climbing the harmonic series. Throat singers in Tuva and Mongolia do the same with their mouths, shaping a formant so sharp that one harmonic rings out above the drone as a second, whistled melody.[^khoomei]

blocks.caption: Two knobs as one square: across is the cutoff, up is the resonance. Drag around it.
blocks.task: Keeping Reso at Q 8 or more, sweep Cutoff through five positions

blocks.text: Cutoff and resonance both change how bright a sound is, which is why they are easily confused by ear. Cutoff moves the edge up and down. Resonance leaves the edge where it is and sharpens it into a peak. When a sound changes, ask whether it got darker or got a peak; it is the most useful question in [PatchMatch](#/ear).

blocks.caption: Cutoff and resonance side by side.
blocks.task: Make it dark and smooth: Cutoff at 500 Hz or lower, Reso at Q 0.7

blocks.text: Now return to the voice from the start of the lesson. Listen to it against the raw buzz and ask the same question: is it darker, or has it got a peak? Both. Most of the top has gone, and there is a hollow, ringing peak like a formant. So the cutoff comes down and the resonance comes up. How far each goes is for your ear to decide.

blocks.caption: The saw and its filter, with the voice to match.
blocks.task: Make the buzz sing like the voice

blocks.text: A single resonant low-pass gives one formant, so it can only suggest a vowel, an “aw” or an “oo”. Two or three peaks moving together, as in the vowel figure above, make speech. Machines that do this from a real voice, the **talk box** and the **vocoder**, put a human mouth on a guitar or a synth.[^vocoder]

blocks.caption: Wendy Carlos in 1985. Her Switched-On Bach of 1968, played on a Moog modular, made the synthesizer famous, and she made a synthesizer sing through a vocoder for A Clockwork Orange.
Six questions on filters and vowels
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: You sing “ee” then “ah” on the same note. What changes?
choices: The shape of the filter your mouth makes
How many times a second your vocal folds open
items.why: The buzz from the vocal folds stays the same; the mouth's resonances, the formants, move.

choices: Resonant peaks of the throat and mouth
The harmonics of the vocal folds
items.why: Each vowel has two or three peaks where the vocal tract rings; those are the formants.

items.ask: What does a low-pass filter do to a saw wave?
choices: Removes the harmonics above the cutoff
Removes the harmonics below the cutoff
items.why: Low-pass lets the low harmonics pass and takes away the high ones. The pitch is the fundamental, which stays.

items.ask: Why does a synth usually start from a saw or pulse, not a sine, before the filter?
choices: A filter can only take away; a sine has nothing above the fundamental to remove
Filters only work on square waves
items.why: Subtractive synthesis needs a rich source. A sine has one harmonic, so a filter has nothing to shape.

items.ask: You turn the resonance right up and sweep the cutoff. What do you hear?
choices: A whistle that picks out one harmonic after another
The pitch of the note sliding up and down
items.why: A ringing peak at the cutoff boosts whichever harmonic it lands on.

items.ask: A sound gets duller, and no peak appears or disappears. Which knob most likely moved?
items.why: Cutoff moves the edge and darkens the sound; resonance adds or removes a peak at the edge.

summary: **A voice is a buzz through a filter**: the vocal folds make a bright buzz and the mouth shapes it.
**Vowels are two or three resonant peaks, the formants.** The jaw moves the first, the tongue the second.
**Kratzenstein's prize tubes (1780)** made vowels from a reed and differently shaped resonators.
**Subtractive synthesis starts bright and takes away.** The filter does the taking.
**A low-pass filter removes harmonics above its cutoff.** Lower cutoff, darker sound, same pitch.
**Resonance boosts a narrow peak at the cutoff**, and at the top it whistles.
**Cutoff darkens; resonance sharpens.** Ask whether a sound got darker or got a peak.

kratzenstein.title: Speaking machines
kratzenstein.text: Eleven years later, in 1791, Wolfgang von Kempelen (better known for the chess-playing Turk, which hid a human player) published a speaking machine with bellows for lungs, a reed for a voice and a leather mouth worked by hand. A young Alexander Graham Bell saw a copy in London and built his own talking head with his brother in Edinburgh.

ladder.title: The Moog ladder
ladder.text: Moog filed for his filter patent in 1966 (it was granted in 1969). It puts four transistor stages in a row, each rolling off 6 decibels per octave above the cutoff, for 24 in all: a steeper edge than most rivals'. Feeding some of the output back to the input gives the resonance, and with enough feedback the filter oscillates as a pure tone.

vocoder.title: Talk boxes and vocoders
vocoder.text: A talk box pipes a guitar's sound up a plastic tube into the player's mouth, which shapes it into vowels for a microphone, as on Peter Frampton's “Show Me the Way” (1975). A vocoder, developed by Homer Dudley at Bell Labs in the 1930s and demonstrated in 1939 to squeeze speech down telephone lines, measures a voice's formants band by band and imposes them on a synth; Wendy Carlos used one for A Clockwork Orange in 1971.

khoomei.title: Overtone singing
khoomei.text: Tuvan khoomei and Mongolian khoomii hold one low drone and move the tongue and lips to tune a sharp formant onto single harmonics, often between the 6th and the 12th, which are close enough together to play a scale. The effect is so clear that listeners often think two people are singing.

q-factor.title: Why Reso is measured in Q
q-factor.text: Engineers measure resonance as *Q* (for “quality factor”): how narrow and tall the peak is compared with its frequency. At Q 0.7 the filter rolls off smoothly with no bump at the cutoff; by Q 8 or 10 it rings with a sharp whistle.
